content.summary: Read about a student who learns through school subjects, practical projects, and performing arts. You will practise finding the main idea and important details, and notice how the present perfect with for and since describes how long something has continued. You will also see polite ways to ask for permission.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Use have or has with a past participle and for plus a period of time, or since plus a starting point. Use Can I...? and May I...? to ask for permission.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Learn words about concentrating, workshops, rehearsals, tiredness, and ways of thinking.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skim the passage first to understand its main idea. Then scan it for names, activities, time expressions, and reasons.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a text about different ways to learn.
Find details about school subjects, after-school activities, and how long they have continued.
Recognize present perfect sentences with for and since.
Identify polite questions and answers about permission.

contextWarmup.prompt: You want to use a school's art room after lessons. What is the best way to ask?
options: May I use the art room after lessons?
I use the art room after lessons yesterday.
The art room is using after lessons.
contextWarmup.explanation: May I...? is a polite way to ask for permission. The other sentences do not make a correct permission request.

rules: Use have or has + past participle + for + a period of time. Example: I have studied English for three years.
Use have or has + past participle + since + the time something started. Example: We have had this workshop since September.
Use for with periods such as a month, three years, or a long time. Use since with starting points such as Friday, 2014, or last summer.
Ask for permission with Can I...? or May I...? A person can give permission with Yes, you can or Of course.

commonTrap.explanation: For tells us how long something has continued. Since tells us when it began. Do not use since with a length of time.
commonTrap.wrong: I have studied science since three years.
commonTrap.correct: I have studied science for three years.

content.passageTitle: More Than One Way to Learn
paragraphs: Maya has been a student at Greenfield School since September, and she has studied English there for six months. She enjoys biology because she can learn about plants and animals. Maths is harder for her, so she asks questions when she does not understand. Her teacher says that drawing a diagram can help her concentrate and remember difficult ideas.

Maya has also attended the school's Friday workshop for three months. Students make useful things from wood and recycled materials. Last week, Maya asked, “May I use the small saw?” Her teacher replied, “Yes, you can, but please wear safety glasses.” Maya has been in the school music group since January, too. She has a rehearsal every Wednesday and sometimes feels exhausted afterwards. She has realised that practising with friends makes learning more enjoyable.

content.summary: Practical guide on using the present perfect tense with for and since, asking and giving permission, and describing school subjects and learning styles in clear English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Present Perfect with For
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have / has + past participle + for + time period
blueprintItems.example: I have studied English for three years.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Present Perfect with Since
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + have / has + past participle + since + specific starting point
blueprintItems.example: Children have made fantastic things since the school started.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Expressing Permission and Requests
blueprintItems.formula: Can / Could / May + subject + base verb + object?
blueprintItems.example: Could I ask a question about our science project?

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'for' with a duration of time and 'since' with a specific starting point.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She has learned French since three years.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She has learned French for three years.
mechanicsRules.why: Three years is a period of time, so you must use 'for' instead of 'since'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize school subjects when they are proper nouns or part of a specific title.
mechanicsRules.badExample: we have history and chemistry on tuesday.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: We have History and Chemistry on Tuesday.
mechanicsRules.why: Days of the week and specific class names are proper nouns in English.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use articles correctly with singular and plural nouns when describing learning materials.
mechanicsRules.badExample: student needs computer to finish project.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: A student needs a computer to finish the project.
mechanicsRules.why: Singular countable nouns require an article like 'a' or 'the'.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: The Ways We Learn

content.summary: This module focuses on speaking clearly when discussing school subjects, study methods, and time durations using the present perfect tense with for and since. Good spoken English at the B1 level requires accurate syllable stress, natural linking between words, and clear articulation of consonant clusters.
content.audioGuidance: Listen carefully to the rhythm of sentences. Notice how weak forms are used for grammatical words like for, since, and have, while key vocabulary words receive strong stress.

pillars.name: Syllable Stress
pillars.target: Correct placement of primary stress in multi-syllable study words
pillars.explanation: Words like concentrate, workshop, and rehearsal have a specific syllable that stands out in loudness and pitch. Getting this right makes your speech instantly understandable.

pillars.name: Present Perfect Linking
pillars.target: Linking auxiliary verbs smoothly with main verbs
pillars.explanation: When speaking quickly, phrases like 'I have studied' sound like 'I've studied'. Pronounce the contracted form clearly to maintain a natural spoken rhythm.

pillars.name: Intonation in Requests
pillars.target: Using rising intonation for polite permission requests
pillars.explanation: When asking for permission to leave a study workshop or borrow a book, raise your pitch slightly at the end of the question to sound polite and engaging.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how the main stress moves when the word changes from a verb to a noun.
Compound nouns usually place primary stress on the first part.
Adding suffixes like -tion shifts the stress to the syllable immediately preceding it.
The stress stays on the root syllable haust across different word forms.
